headline: AI Companies Slash Prices as Competition Heats Up

levels.label: Grade 3-4
levels.summary: Big companies that make AI chatbots, like OpenAI and Anthropic, are lowering their prices. This is happening because other companies, especially some from China, made their own AI tools that work well but cost less money. When you use an AI chatbot, the company charges money based on how much text goes in and how much text comes out. These little pieces of text are called 'tokens.' Think of tokens like coins you pay with every time the AI reads your question or writes an answer. OpenAI cut its prices a lot for one of its AI tools. Anthropic did something similar with a new AI tool called Opus 5. However, the companies are not lowering prices on their very best, most powerful AI tools. Those stay expensive. Experts say this shows the companies want to keep charging a lot for their top products while competing hard for everyday, cheaper AI tools. This matters because cheaper AI could mean cheaper tools for schools, businesses, and everyday people in the future.

levels.label: Grade 5-6
levels.summary: Two major American AI companies, OpenAI and Anthropic, are cutting prices on their AI chatbot tools. This is a response to growing competition from Chinese AI companies, like DeepSeek and Moonshot, whose tools are cheaper but still perform well. When people or businesses use an AI chatbot, they pay for 'tokens'—units used to measure the text going into the AI (called input) and the text the AI creates in response (called output). OpenAI dropped the price of one of its tools by a huge amount, both for input and output tokens. Anthropic released a new tool, Opus 5, priced at half the cost of its previous top model. Anthropic also canceled a planned price increase for another one of its tools. However, pricing isn't simple. Some AI tools can solve problems using fewer tokens or fewer tries, which can make an expensive-looking tool actually cheaper to use overall. Also, AI tools can run at different 'effort levels'—kind of like choosing how hard the AI thinks about a problem—which changes both how well it performs and how much it costs. Researchers found that some cheaper Chinese AI tools running at high effort performed similarly to American tools, but for less money. Even so, the priciest, most powerful AI models from top companies aren't getting cheaper. Experts say this shows companies are competing hard on affordable tools while trying to protect the value of their best, most expensive ones.

levels.label: Grade 7-8
levels.summary: OpenAI and Anthropic, two leading American artificial intelligence companies, are cutting prices on some of their AI chatbot products as competition intensifies from Chinese AI companies such as DeepSeek and Moonshot. AI companies charge customers based on 'tokens'—units that measure the amount of text put into a chatbot (input) and the amount of text it generates back (output). OpenAI reduced the price of one of its mid-level tools dramatically, cutting input token costs to a fifth of the original price and output costs to a fifth as well. Anthropic launched a new model called Opus 5 priced at half the cost of its previous flagship model, and it also canceled a planned price hike for another product line. These cuts specifically target the 'mid-tier' market—AI tools that aren't the most advanced but are affordable and widely used—making them more competitive with cheaper Chinese alternatives. However, comparing AI prices isn't as simple as looking at token costs. A more capable AI model might solve a task using fewer tokens or fewer attempts, so a tool that looks pricier per token could end up costing less overall to complete a job. AI companies also let customers choose different 'effort settings,' which control how much computing power the AI uses to answer a question—similar to choosing between a quick guess and a careful, thorough answer. Higher effort settings usually mean better results but higher costs. Research from a group called Artificial Analysis found that some AI tools set to a lower effort level performed about as well, and cost about the same per task, as competitor tools running at maximum effort. This means simple price comparisons between AI companies can be misleading. Notably, prices for the very best, most advanced AI models are staying the same or even rising, according to one technology expert. This suggests companies are willing to compete fiercely on affordable, everyday AI tools while protecting the price and profit of their top-tier, most powerful products. This pricing battle matters because it could make AI tools more accessible and affordable for regular people, schools, and businesses, while showing how global competition, especially from China, is reshaping the AI industry.

levels.label: Grade 9-10
levels.summary: A price war is unfolding in the artificial intelligence industry as leading American companies OpenAI and Anthropic cut prices on their AI chatbot products to compete with increasingly capable and cheaper AI tools from Chinese companies like DeepSeek and Moonshot. AI companies typically charge customers based on 'tokens,' units that measure both the text fed into a model (input) and the text the model generates in response (output). Costs also vary depending on which version of a model is used and its 'effort' setting, which adjusts how much computing power is applied to a task. OpenAI slashed prices on one of its mid-tier tools, cutting input token costs to a fifth of their original price and output costs to a fifth as well. Anthropic introduced a new model, Opus 5, priced at half the cost of its previous flagship offering, and separately canceled a planned price increase for another product that had been scheduled to take effect this fall. These moves specifically target the mid-range AI market, where affordability matters most to everyday users and businesses, rather than the premium tier of the most advanced AI systems. Importantly, comparing prices across AI companies isn't straightforward. A model that costs more per token might still be cheaper overall if it can complete a task using fewer tokens or fewer attempts, since efficiency affects total cost as much as headline pricing does. Additionally, effort settings—which control how much computational power a model uses—affect both accuracy and cost, making direct price comparisons even trickier. A research firm called Artificial Analysis, which benchmarks AI models on tasks like math, science, and coding, found that some AI tools running at a moderate effort level performed comparably, in both quality and cost, to competitor tools running at their maximum setting. In one comparison, an OpenAI model at maximum effort matched the performance of a Chinese DeepSeek model at maximum effort, but cost nearly twice as much per completed task. Despite these mid-tier cuts, prices for the most advanced, flagship AI models from top companies remain stable or are even increasing, according to an AI technology expert who has used these systems since 2020. He suggested this pricing pattern reveals a deliberate strategy: American AI labs are willing to compete aggressively on affordable, everyday products while defending the premium pricing of their top-performing systems. This dynamic matters broadly because it signals how global competition, particularly from China, is reshaping affordability and access to AI technology, potentially benefiting everyday consumers, students, and businesses who rely on cheaper AI tools for tasks ranging from writing help to customer service.

levels.label: Grade 11+
levels.summary: The artificial intelligence industry is experiencing an intensifying price war, as leading American AI developers OpenAI and Anthropic slash prices on select chatbot products to fend off increasingly competitive and affordable offerings from Chinese rivals such as DeepSeek and Moonshot. AI companies generally charge customers based on 'tokens,' the units used to measure both the text submitted to a model (input) and the text it generates in response (output), with pricing also fluctuating according to model version and 'effort' settings that determine how much computational power is devoted to a given task. In this latest round of cuts, OpenAI reduced pricing on one of its mid-tier products dramatically, dropping input token costs to a fifth of their previous rate and output costs to a fifth as well. Anthropic, meanwhile, launched a new model called Opus 5 priced at half the cost of its existing flagship offering, and separately reversed course on a planned price increase for another model that had been scheduled to take effect this fall. Notably, these price reductions are concentrated in the mid-tier segment of the market—products aimed at cost-conscious customers and everyday applications—rather than the premium, flagship-level AI systems that represent the cutting edge of each company's technology. This distinction matters because comparing AI pricing across companies based solely on token costs can be misleading. A model with a higher per-token price may still prove cheaper to use overall if it can complete tasks using fewer tokens or fewer attempts, meaning efficiency, not just sticker price, determines real-world cost. Compounding this complexity, most AI models can operate at different 'effort' settings, which adjust computational power and, consequently, both the quality of results and the total cost of completing a task. Independent benchmarking firm Artificial Analysis, which evaluates AI models across domains including mathematics, science, coding, and reasoning, found that Anthropic's Opus 5 running at a 'medium' effort setting delivered performance and cost efficiency comparable to Moonshot's Kimi K3 running at its maximum effort setting. Similarly, OpenAI's mid-tier model at maximum effort matched the performance of a DeepSeek model at maximum effort, yet cost nearly double per completed task—illustrating how headline pricing alone fails to capture true value. Despite these aggressive cuts to mid-tier offerings, pricing for each company's most advanced, top-performing models has remained flat or even increased, according to an AI technology lead at a web hosting company who has used large language models professionally since 2020. He characterized the current moment as the first genuine test of whether major AI labs can preserve premium pricing for their flagship products while competing fiercely on affordability elsewhere, summarizing the strategy succinctly: companies are cutting prices in the middle of their product lineups while defending the value of their top-tier offerings. This pricing strategy carries significant real-world implications, as it suggests that global competitive pressure, particularly from Chinese AI developers, is reshaping affordability across the industry, potentially expanding access to AI tools for cost-sensitive consumers, students, and businesses, even as the most cutting-edge AI capabilities remain a premium, closely guarded commodity.

questions: If AI tools become cheaper for everyday use but the most powerful ones stay expensive, who do you think benefits most from that arrangement, and who might be left behind?
How might competition between American and Chinese AI companies affect the tools you or your school might use in the future?
Why do you think it's tricky to compare prices between different AI companies just by looking at their sticker prices, and why might that matter for consumers trying to make good choices?
